guides.title: Android phone or tablet (Android 12 and newer)

sections.title: Back up what you want to keep

steps.text: Open Settings > Google > All services > Backup, then tap Back up now.
steps.detail: This saves apps and app data, call history, contacts, settings and SMS to your Google Account. Photos and videos are backed up by the Google Photos app.

steps.text: Wait for the backup to finish before you go further.
steps.detail: Google says a backup can take up to 24 hours to finish. You get 15 GB of storage at no charge.

sources.title: Back up or restore data on your Android device

sections.title: Save your WhatsApp chats

steps.text: In WhatsApp, tap the three dots > Settings > Chats > Chat backup > Back up.
steps.detail: Your chats are saved to your Google Account. You need a Google Account on the phone, Google Play services, enough free space, and a steady internet connection. Use Wi-Fi to avoid mobile data charges.

steps.text: Optional: turn on End-to-end encrypted backup in the same Chat backup screen.
steps.detail: Choose a passkey, a password or a 64-digit key. WhatsApp says it is the only way to open your backup later, so write it down somewhere safe.

sources.title: How to back up your chat history (Android)

sections.title: Get ready before the reset

steps.text: Note your Google Account email and make sure you know its password.
steps.detail: Check it by signing in on another phone or computer. Google asks for this information after a reset.

steps.text: Keep your phone's PIN, pattern or password handy.
Changed your Google password recently? Wait 24 hours before resetting.
steps.detail: Google's advice for anyone who reset their Google Account password in the last 24 hours.

steps.text: Charge the phone to at least 70% and connect to Wi-Fi or mobile data.
steps.detail: Google says a reset can take up to an hour.

steps.text: Nothing to switch on for encryption.
steps.detail: Google's Android security documentation says full-disk encryption is not allowed on new devices running Android 10 and higher; they use file-based encryption instead. The factory reset then removes your data.

sources.title: Reset your Android device to factory settings
Encryption (Android Open Source Project)

sections.title: Remove your Google Account (turns off Factory Reset Protection)

steps.text: Open Settings > Passwords & accounts (or Accounts), tap your Google Account, tap Remove account and confirm.
steps.detail: On some phones the menu is called Users & accounts or Manage accounts. You will need your PIN, pattern or password.

steps.text: Do this before the reset, not after.
steps.detail: Google says removing your Google Account turns off device protection. If you skip it, the phone asks for your account after the reset and nobody else can use it.

steps.text: Remove any other accounts listed there (email, work and so on) the same way.
steps.detail: Removing an account also deletes its email, contacts and settings from the phone.

sections.title: Take out your SIM, eSIM and memory card

steps.text: Erase your eSIM: open Settings > Network & internet > Mobile network (or SIMs), pick the eSIM, tap Erase eSIM.
steps.detail: Menu names vary by brand. If you can't find it, ask your mobile operator to move or deactivate the eSIM. Some steps need Android 11 or later.

steps.text: Switch the phone off and take your SIM card out of the tray.
steps.detail: Google's trade-in steps say to remove the SIM card but leave the empty tray in the phone.

steps.text: Take out the microSD memory card, if there is one.
steps.detail: Google warns that erasing a phone may not delete SD cards. Keep the card, or wipe it using the Loose drives guide.

sections.title: Factory reset the phone

steps.text: Open Settings > System > Reset options > Erase all data (factory reset), then tap Erase all data.
steps.detail: This is the path on Google Pixel phones; other brands use similar menu names. Enter your PIN if asked.

steps.text: If Settings won't open, use the power and volume buttons method from your phone maker's support site.
steps.detail: Google says most phones are reset from Settings; the button method varies by manufacturer.

steps.text: When the phone restarts, check that it does not ask for your password or Google Account.
steps.detail: Google says that if it still asks, the reset is not complete and you must do it again.

steps.text: Switch the phone off. It is ready to hand over.

sections.title: Remove the phone from your Google Account online

steps.text: Go to myaccount.google.com > Security & sign-in > Manage all devices, tap the old phone and tap Sign out.
steps.detail: Do this from any phone or computer. Google advises signing out on devices that are no longer yours. If several entries share the same name, sign out of all of them.

guides.note: Feature phones differ a lot. Steps follow HMD's official Nokia feature-phone guide (closest official source) and NIST's note that a factory reset is the accepted 'Clear' method for basic phones. Treat menu names as generic.

steps.detail: On the Nokia 105 (2023), type *#7370# on the home screen and enter the security code. HMD says this removes all data saved in the phone memory.

steps.text: After the restart, open Contacts, Messages and the call log and check they are empty.
steps.detail: Delete anything that is left by hand. NIST advises checking that a wipe actually worked.

guides.title: Loose drives: hard disk, SSD, USB stick, memory card

sections.title: Three levels of wiping (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2)

steps.text: Clear: erase with normal tools, such as overwriting the whole drive or a factory reset.
steps.detail: Protects against simple, non-invasive recovery using the drive's normal connection.

steps.text: Purge: use the drive's own secure-erase or sanitize command, or delete the encryption key (cryptographic erase).
steps.detail: Makes recovery infeasible even with lab techniques and keeps the drive usable. NIST says to use Purge instead of Clear when possible.

steps.text: Destroy: shred, crush to powder, melt or burn the drive so it can never be used again.
steps.detail: NIST says this may be the only option when a drive has failed or is too old to connect.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization
sources.publisher: NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology)

sections.title: Working hard disk (HDD)

steps.text: Overwrite the whole drive once with a disk-wipe tool (Clear), or use its secure-erase command (Purge).
steps.detail: NIST says overwriting typically stops recovery even with lab techniques; the old many-pass routines are past practice.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization
sources.publisher: NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology)

sections.title: SSD, USB stick or memory card

steps.text: Don't rely on overwriting or deleting files.
steps.detail: NIST says flash storage keeps spare cells and spreads out writes, so overwriting cannot reach all old data. Degaussing also does not work on flash.

steps.text: Use the maker's secure-erase or sanitize tool, or erase the encryption key if the drive was encrypted.
steps.detail: This is Purge. If you can't do that, have the drive destroyed.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization
sources.publisher: NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology)

sections.title: Dead or damaged drives

steps.text: Don't hand over a dead drive as-is. Have it physically destroyed (shredded or pulverised).
steps.detail: NIST says overwriting can't be used on a drive that is damaged or no longer works, so destruction may be the only option.

steps.text: Ask your recycler for a record of what was destroyed.
steps.detail: NIST includes a sample sanitization certificate with make, serial number and method.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization
sources.publisher: NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology)

sections.title: Check your work

steps.text: Plug the drive in after wiping and check that your old files are gone.
steps.detail: NIST says checking the result is an important part of wiping.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization
sources.publisher: NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology)

sections.title: Unlink your bank accounts from UPI apps

steps.text: In Google Pay, tap your profile picture > Bank account, pick the account, tap More > Remove account.
steps.detail: Unlink any active autopay or UPI Lite on that account first; Google Pay won't remove it otherwise.

steps.text: Don't rely on signing out, uninstalling or resetting.
steps.detail: Google Pay says your account and the UPI IDs you created stay active and linked to your bank after sign-out, uninstall or factory reset.

steps.text: Repeat in every other UPI or bank app on the phone (PhonePe, Paytm, BHIM, your bank's app).
steps.detail: General advice: menus differ per app. Check each app's help section.

steps.text: Then sign out: Google Pay > profile picture > Settings > Sign out.
Take out the SIM linked to your bank account and keep it.
steps.detail: General advice: UPI works through the mobile number registered with your bank. Google's trade-in steps also say to remove the SIM card.

sections.title: Smart TV or streaming box (example: Google TV)

steps.text: Open Settings > System > About > Factory reset.
steps.detail: Google says a factory reset erases all your data from the device. Other TV brands have a similar option; check your brand's support site.

sections.title: Wi-Fi router (example: TP-Link)

steps.text: With the router on, hold the Reset button for more than 10 seconds until the SYS light flashes quickly.
steps.detail: On a combined WPS/Reset button, holding it for less than 5 seconds only starts WPS. Some routers have a pinhole that needs a pin or paperclip.

steps.text: Or log in at tplinkwifi.net, go to Advanced > System Tools > Backup and Restore and click Factory Restore.
steps.detail: This erases your Wi-Fi name and password, internet login and other settings. Keep the router powered on until it restarts.

sections.title: Printer (example: HP LaserJet Pro)

steps.text: On the touchscreen, open Setup > Printer Maintenance > Restore > Restore Factory Defaults.
steps.detail: HP says this returns all printer and network settings to factory defaults and deletes pages stored in memory. Menus differ on other models.

steps.text: Change or remove the printer's admin (EWS) password separately.
steps.detail: HP says a factory reset does not reset the Embedded Web Server password.

steps.text: Stop using a battery that is swollen, hot, leaking, smelly, discoloured or has changed shape.
steps.detail: US EPA says swelling means the battery is damaged and is a fire hazard.

steps.text: Don't charge it or switch the device on.
steps.detail: The US Fire Administration says to stop using a battery that shows these signs.

steps.text: Don't press, bend, puncture or try to open it.
steps.detail: EPA warns that damaged or crushed lithium batteries can start fires.

steps.text: Cover the metal terminals with electrical tape and put each battery or device in its own plastic bag.
Keep it out of sunlight and hot places, away from anything that can burn.
steps.detail: EPA suggests storing a swollen battery in a container of sand or somewhere away from flammable things until you can hand it over.

steps.text: Never put it in the household dustbin or dry-waste bag. Give it to an e-waste collector or recycler.
steps.detail: For a damaged battery, EPA advises asking the device maker or seller how to handle it.

steps.text: If it smokes or catches fire, move away and call emergency services.
steps.detail: US EPA says to call emergency services if there is an immediate fire risk.
